# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

No Launch HN exists (HN search for Veles finds no launch thread: https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=Veles&tags=story).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

insights_note: no grouping to read (no follow-up line with two answers)

founder.order_why: The four steps run in a sensible line from context to problem to solution to launch, but screens 21 and 22 ask how account executives should answer and who gets a link after the kicker already says the interviews are sent, when those choices belong before sending, beside screen 20.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the identical kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context step reads as asked twice around the recency screen 4; screen 2 (where you sell) also overlaps the 'where: US' field the context step holds.
founder.missing: Nothing asks the commercial side: my price ($250 to $500 per sales team a month), the unit it is charged per (a sales team of up to ten), who decides and pays (the sales director, with the CFO agreeing the discount rules), what the problem costs today (deals lost or signed on worse terms), or what a buyer must clear to buy (the CRM check, a security review). Sales directors are meant to get their own Part 3 link, yet no screen asks who they are or what to ask them, and 'Offer a pilot?' is asked without any price for the pilot to be set against.

PRIMARY.order_why: Asking whether my last deal was already set up in the CRM after the idea card feels out of place, since it's a fact about my recent work that belongs back in Part 1 before I'm shown Veles, not between the idea and my reaction to it.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked how long the approval wait actually was or what slowed it down (who had to sign off, how many people I had to chase), and nothing asked how I build quotes today in spreadsheets, Slides and email chains, or how hard the pricing rules were to find, so the switching question on screen 5 has nothing to stand on.

screens.why1: Naming the project is the obvious first step of setting up a study, before anything about the idea is asked.
screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain to any founder on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my own company's name and how I describe it, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options, rows or chips to judge.
screens.why5: The name I typed, "Veles — a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams", is kept exactly, and since this is a founder-side screen nothing leaks to respondents.

screens.why1: Right after naming the project, asking where I sell first is the obvious next setup step, since it sets the market for everything after it.
screens.why2: "Where will you sell this first?" is plain to any founder, and a country plus optional region is exactly how I would answer.
screens.why3: I know my launch market cold: US software companies, where my team and every testimonial sit.
screens.why4: A country picker with an optional region covers my true answer, US with no region, and nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: US with no region is exactly what my material says, and the kicker names Veles as I described it, with nothing reaching respondents.

screens.why1: Pinning down who, what job, when and which teams is the obvious first step before Keel tests anything, and it comes right after naming the project and choosing the US market.

screens.why1: After asking how it fits and what it does better, asking what my reps must change to start is the obvious next question about adoption, and I know my reps' habits well enough to answer it.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is how I'd describe rolling out a quoting tool to a sales team, so I read it once and typed my answer.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we ask of an AE: quote in our calculator instead of their Google Sheets and log concessions as the deal is negotiated.
screens.why4: A free-text box with a 25-word cap fits a two-part answer, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right escape if I don't want adoption tested.
screens.why5: The belief Keel shows keeps 'build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets' word for word but drops 'record each concession as the deal is negotiated', which is half of what I typed and the part reps will push back on.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? (e.g. quote every deal in the calculator instead of spreadsheets; log each concession as they negotiate). Keep both parts in the belief, or say plainly that only the first will be tested.

screens.why1: Right after I said what reps will have to do to start, Keel shows back the steps it drafted from my words, which is exactly the check I expect here.
screens.why2: The rows are plain sales-floor language (quote, calculator, concession), but the intro repeats the title word for word ('What they'll have to do. What they'll have to do'), which reads like a glitch and costs a second read.
screens.why3: Whether my reps will give up their pricing sheets and log concessions mid-negotiation is the adoption question I live with every demo.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct, they are the two real changes my tool asks of a rep, and neither is odd or missing (the CRM fit was already covered under compatibility).
screens.why5: Both rows are my own launch claims (every quote in one calculator, track the concessions), and the belief tests the one that matters most, held as I typed it.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do. Reword, remove or add; under 9 words each. You pick the one to test next. — Build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets / Record each concession as the deal is negotiated

screens.why1: Right after I checked the two adoption efforts Keel wrote, it asks me to pick the one to test, which is the obvious next step before the fourth solution test.
screens.why2: "Which one is most likely to stop them?" over my own two efforts reads at first glance, and quote, calculator, spreadsheets and concession are everyday words on a deal desk.
screens.why3: I know from every rep I've sold to that ripping them off their Google Sheets is the real hurdle, far more than logging concessions, so I can answer this from what I've seen.
screens.why4: The two options are exactly the two efforts I typed, they are distinct, and no third one is missing since the CRM fit was already tested under Compatibility.
screens.why5: The belief and the test keep my words verbatim, "build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets", and the bar of no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no is a fair read of "most would".

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, deciding whether to ask strangers for a trial is the natural last step, and for me a trial on one team's live deals is exactly the commitment I want to find.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is everyday B2B sales language, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want early pilot leads is entirely my own call as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the complete, distinct choice here and both are in plain words.
screens.why5: The meaning is kept, but "try this for real, leave your email" reads as a consumer sign-up, while my real next step is a demo or a trial on one sales team's deals, and the decision sits with the sales director rather than the rep answering.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents who say yes see: "Would your team try this on its live deals? Leave your work email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer's voice right before sending is the obvious last setup step, and it hasn't been asked before.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs four ideas (video, typed fallback, a one-off 400-credit recording, text-message delivery) into one paragraph I'd read twice, and 'credits' isn't explained.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice my AEs would take a call from; I just need to hear both samples.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a 5-second sample and a default preselected, is all the choice needs.
screens.why5: It says 'account executives' as I typed it and leaks nothing about Veles to the reps.
screens.instead: Who should ask account executives your questions? (Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s) — hint: 'Daphne is picked; tap Saskia to hear her. Recording either voice costs 400 credits, once.'

screens.why1: Choosing how my account executives answer belongs just before sending, but right after 'Who should ask account executives your questions?' it reads as nearly the same question asked twice, and the 'SENT' kicker is odd when nothing has been sent yet.
screens.why2: The three choices are clear, but 'Hear her' and 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' run into the option text and take a second read to see they are a link and a status.
screens.why3: I know AEs live in a calendar of calls, and whether they would sit for a video interviewer or tap through between meetings is a call I can make from my own team.
screens.why4: AI voice, text, or let them pick covers every real way to answer, each is distinct, and the readiness note on each tells me what I am waiting on.
screens.why5: It speaks of account executives as I typed them, and nothing of Veles or its pricing calculator leaks into the respondent-facing description.
screens.instead: Ask once, merged with the previous screen: 'How should account executives answer? — Talk to Daphne, our AI interviewer (video, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let each one choose', with 'Hear Daphne' as a separate link.

screens.why1: After choosing how account executives answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen and clear enough in context.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching AEs I know by name, a list, or a community like a RevOps Slack, so I can answer from what I do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real options, but the open-link option's Google sign-in is a detail that may put off AEs in a Slack group and overlaps a little with 'found with Keel' when I'd post to a list I built.
screens.why5: Nothing of Veles or my roles is changed or leaked; it is purely about distribution and my pick, each AE by name, is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is plain, but the line beside it gives only 'Compatibility: 4 answered'; the bar of 5 sits down on the cards, and the header's '7 people answered' clashes with the 4 without saying why 3 dropped out.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, only the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered'; '5 needed' is clear on each card, but I need a second look to see why 7 answered and only 4 count on every belief.
screens.why_b3: All three names and belief lines (deal already in the CRM, same-day quote, every quote in the calculator) are exactly the ones I checked, though Keel's run-on statement above them repeats itself and reads badly.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not how many more account executives I need to reach 5 on each belief, not who the 3 uncounted people were, and not whether to send the study out again.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing about my solution and openly says each belief is too thin to call at 4 of 5 needed.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 7 account executives answered but only 4 reached the solution questions (3 stopped earlier); one more per belief gets you to 5, so send the study to about 3 more reps before reading these.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '5 needed to call it', but the line under it says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', so I have to work out that it means 4 counted.
screens.why_b2: I can see 3 yes, 1 yes with some steps and 0 no out of 4, with the bar at 3 of 4, but the bar is put as '3 of 4' for me and also as 'no more than 1 in 3 say no', so I read it twice to check those are the same bar.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, and 'For most account executives, the deal was already set up in the CRM' is word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that every counted rep was for me or that one more counted answer would settle it.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible throughout, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and a 4-of-4 lean is not claimed as held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted reps had the deal in the CRM (3 outright, 1 with some steps), one short of the 5 needed. Get one more rep's answer before reading this as held.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right above "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I can see the verdict and the count that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: I can see what is counted (3 a lot better, 1 no difference, over 4), but the doubled numbers ("Better · 3 3") and a bar written both as "3 of 4" and "no more than 1 in 3" took me a second look to place the marker.
screens.why_b3: The title is Relative advantage and the belief is my line word for word: the quote built and approved the same day.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" doesn't tell me to get one more rep's answer, or that the one no came from a rep whose CPQ already quotes in minutes.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, and 3 of 4 is never dressed up as a hold.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 account executives said a lot better and 1 said no difference (his CPQ already quotes in minutes); one more counted answer would settle it, so send the study to another rep.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside "4 answered · 5 needed", but the count line below says 5 answered and 4 counted, so the number beside the verdict should read "4 counted" to match what decides it.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the for/against cells are plain, but "your bar · 3 of 4" with the marker at 3 reads as if 3 of 4 were the bar, not the result; I had to work out that 1 against in 4 sits under the 1-in-3 ceiling.
screens.why_b3: The card says Adoption friction and "Most would build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets", exactly what I checked.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it doesn't say that one more counted answer would call it, or that the lean is 3 for and 1 against, with Mateo's CPQ-holding team the one against.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, says the group is small, calls the result a lean not a call, and claims nothing beyond the five who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 counted (Mei-Ling's was a guess), 5 needed; it leans your way at 3 for and 1 against, so one more clear answer from a rep would settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b3: The name 'Relative advantage' and the belief line are exactly what I checked: the quote built and approved the same day.
screens.why_b4: The 5-needed line implies 'get one more answer', but nothing says what Mateo's CPQ point means for the idea, such as checking whether teams that already run a CPQ are outside my segment.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (4 answered, 1 against, 1 asked), and no claim goes beyond a single quote.
screens.why_b6: Mateo's line tells me something I did not type: where the price book already lives in a CPQ, quoting takes minutes and the rep's pain is pipeline and forecast, so same-day approval is no advantage for CPQ teams.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5 needed). The one 'no difference' comes from a rep whose CPQ already quotes in minutes, so ask whether teams with a CPQ belong in your segment and get one more answer.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it makes sense to check first whether I actually hit an approval wait on a quote this month before asking me about it.
screens.why2: Waiting on pricing approval for a quote is everyday language on my team; I'd answer it instantly, though I'd say 'customer' or 'prospect' more than 'buyer'.
screens.why3: Whether I sat waiting on deal desk or my VP to sign off on a discount in the last four weeks is something I know cold.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, and here there are two: 'I'd rather not say' isn't allowed, and 'I can't recall one particular enterprise deal' answers a different question than whether I waited.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's two-day approval wait on a quote in plain sales terms, without leaking any product or plan.
screens.why6: Spoken as one short question followed by 'Yes or no', it's easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, did you wait on pricing approval before sending a customer a quote? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I waited on pricing approval for a quote, showing me an idea about building and pricing quotes is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: CRM, CPQ, deal desk, standard terms and discounting are words I use every day, though 'a quote with deal benchmarks' as a name for the thing is a bit clumsy.
screens.why3: Building quotes, chasing deal desk rules and fighting over discounts is exactly my week, so I can react to this from what I do.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The last line about leadership seeing how every deal was priced and negotiated, and 'less discounting', reads like the pitch to my VP rather than to me, and to a rep it sounds like being watched.
screens.why6: It says mostly fine, but 'a pricing calculator integrated with your CRM and CPQ' is a mouthful in one breath and the second sentence runs long when heard.
screens.instead: Imagine Veles, a quoting tool that shows how comparable deals were priced. You build the quote inside your CRM, with the deal desk rules and standard terms already in it. The people building it believe it would get your quote priced right and approved without the back-and-forth.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it makes sense to check whether my deal would already be in the CRM for a quote tool to pull from, though the switch from 'buyer's quote' to 'last enterprise deal' is a small hop.
screens.why2: Enterprise deal and CRM are my everyday words, and I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I key my own deals into the CRM by hand, so I know whether that last one was set up or not.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' doesn't fit 'was it already set up': a deal is in the CRM or it isn't, so the middle option means nothing here, and 'partly, some fields missing' would be the real in-between.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks past the card, but asking whether the deal was set up in the CRM drifts a little from whether the deal's details would be there for a benchmarked quote.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and three options plus the escape are easy to hold by ear.
screens.instead: Think of your last enterprise deal. Were its details already in your CRM when you built the quote? Yes, all of them · Some, I had to add the rest · No, none · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the CRM question, asking whether Veles would have helped my last enterprise deal is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but 'go better for you' is loose: better could mean a faster approval, a price I could defend, or a bigger deal, so I'd have to pick one in my head first.
screens.why3: My last enterprise deal and how pricing and approval went on it are things I actually lived through, so I can judge it.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits when I don't know enough about the tool.
screens.why5: It asks about what the founder is after, getting a deal priced and approved with backing, and the idea is shown on purpose on the card, so nothing leaks in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options read as a list and one escape at the end, so I can hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: Would Veles have made pricing and getting approval on your last enterprise deal go better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether Veles would have helped my last deal, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually move my quoting out of Sheets to use it, since that is the real cost for me.
screens.why2: Building quotes in spreadsheets is exactly what I do every week, so 'build every quote in it, not in spreadsheets' reads straight off on the first pass.
screens.why3: I know how I build quotes today in Google Sheets and Slides, so I can say from my own habits whether I'd switch.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: 'Yes' and 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' both lean yes against 'Probably not' and 'No', there is no 'Probably yes', and nearly any rep would pick the conditional yes, so the first two blur together.
screens.why5: 'A quote with deal benchmarks' is an odd way to name a product, because a quote is something I send a buyer, not a tool I use, so the card drifts from what the thing actually is.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold in my head and a single escape at the end, and it sounds natural when said aloud.
screens.instead: To use Veles, you'd build every quote in it instead of in spreadsheets. Would you do that, or not? Options: Yes, for every quote · Yes, for the bigger deals only · Probably not · No; escape: I can't tell
